item.title: Misil impacta sede de Saudi Aramco, mientras recrudece conflicto de Riad con los hutíes
item.description: Un misil balístico impactó en la sede de la petrolera estatal de Arabia Saudita, la mayor del mundo y pilar fundamental de la economía del reino, informó a Reuters una fuente de la empresa, en medio de una guerra cada vez más intensa entre los hutíes de Yemen y una coalición liderada por Riad.
item.dc:creator: Timour Azhari, Menna Alaaeldin
item.content:encoded: Un misil balístico impactó en la sede de la petrolera estatal de Arabia Saudita, la mayor del mundo y pilar fundamental de la economía del reino, informó a Reuters una fuente de la empresa, en medio de una guerra cada vez más intensa entre los hutíes de Yemen y una coalición liderada por Riad. Una torre de oficinas del complejo de Saudi Aramco, situado en la ciudad oriental de Dhahran, fue alcanzada el martes por la noche y las tres plantas superiores resultaron dañadas, según la fuente. La fuente y otras dos personas con conocimiento del asunto afirmaron que el edificio estaba en llamas. El complejo alberga un importante centro de operaciones de Aramco, que supervisa una vasta red de plataformas petrolíferas en tierra y mar, oleoductos, refinerías y terminales de exportación. Anteriormente, seis fuentes habían declarado a Reuters que habían oído fuertes estruendos cerca del complejo. No hubo ningún comentario oficial por parte de Saudi Aramco. La coalición liderada por Arabia Saudita afirmó que fragmentos de un misil que había interceptado y destruido en Dhahran habían caído sobre una zona residencial, sin dar más detalles. Las autoridades también informaron que se habían interceptado y destruido drones y misiles en Riad y en la región sur del país. Los hutíes habían amenazado anteriormente con una respuesta "dura y dolorosa" a los ataques liderados por Arabia Saudita contra la capital yemení, Saná, y su portavoz, Yahya Saree, afirmó que entre los objetivos podrían figurar la sede de Saudi Aramco en Dhahran y una refinería de petróleo en Riad. El grupo ha advertido a los trabajadores del sector petrolero de Arabia Saudita que se mantengan alejados de las instalaciones que podrían ser objeto de ataques. Los hutíes llevan una semana lanzando ataques contra aeropuertos saudíes, incluido uno el sábado en Riad que causó la muerte de 13 personas, en represalia por el apoyo del reino a las fuerzas gubernamentales en la reavivada guerra civil de Yemen. Los hutíes afirmaron el martes por la mañana que Arabia Saudita estaba atacando Saná, y la coalición liderada por Riad advirtió a la población civil que se mantuviera alejada de un depósito de petróleo situado en las afueras de la ciudad. La cadena de televisión Al-Masirah, controlada por los hutíes, informó que la coalición liderada por Riad atacó la estación central de Sabah de la Compañía Petrolera de Yemen (YPC), un depósito de combustible situado en las afueras de Saná. La YPC dijo que la instalación no albergaba en ese momento existencias de productos petroleros y que el ataque no afecta a las reservas de crudo ni a las cadenas de suministro. El Consejo de Ministros saudí, presidido por el gobernante de facto, el príncipe heredero Mohammed bin Salman, emitió un comunicado en el que dijo que los hutíes afrontarán las consecuencias de sus repetidos ataques contra el reino. El bombardeo con misiles balísticos del sábado contra el aeropuerto de Riad ha sido el más mortífero en Arabia Saudita en una década, y los nuevos ataques han provocado la suspensión de vuelos en todo el país, justo cuando este acoge una importante conferencia sobre energía.

item.title: Papa León XIV es diagnosticado con cáncer luego de que médicos remueven parte de pulmón: Vaticano
item.description: El Papa León XIV fue diagnosticado con cáncer de pulmón, después de que los médicos le extirparan el lóbulo inferior del pulmón derecho en una intervención quirúrgica realizada el martes, informó el Vaticano, lo que supone un importante revés para la salud del pontífice de 71 años.
item.dc:creator: Joshua McElwee, Matteo Negri
item.content:encoded: El Papa León XIV fue diagnosticado con cáncer de pulmón, después de que los médicos le extirparan el lóbulo inferior del pulmón derecho en una intervención quirúrgica realizada el martes, informó el Vaticano, lo que supone un importante revés para la salud del pontífice de 71 años. León padece adenocarcinoma pulmonar, una forma común de cáncer de pulmón. Los análisis de tejido realizados durante la operación confirmaron las sospechas que los médicos tenían tras los exámenes preliminares, indicó el boletín médico. León XIV ingresó el martes en el hospital Gemelli de Roma para someterse a una cirugía destinada a extirpar una masa pulmonar detectada durante una revisión médica reciente. El Vaticano había anunciado previamente el martes que la operación había sido un éxito, antes de ofrecer información más detallada por parte del cirujano principal, el profesor Stefano Margaritora, jefe de cirugía torácica del Gemelli. "Para lograr un efecto curativo, se extirpó el lóbulo inferior del pulmón derecho mediante una técnica asistida por video", señaló el informe de Margaritora. "Un análisis histológico intraoperatorio rápido confirmó el diagnóstico de adenocarcinoma pulmonar, tal como se sospechaba a raíz de las pruebas preoperatorias", añadió. La intervención del martes duró unos 90 minutos y se desarrolló con éxito y sin complicaciones, informó el Vaticano. El papa despertó con normalidad y descansa en su habitación del hospital. El comunicado no ofreció más detalles. UNA SEMANA HOSPITALIZADO León salió del Vaticano antes de la intervención, poco antes de las 1100 GMT en Roma, y se le vio saludando con la mano desde la parte trasera de un todoterreno negro mientras su comitiva recorría unos 9 km al norte del Vaticano hasta llegar al Gemelli. Al llegar al hospital, León estrechó la mano a varios funcionarios, pasó ante una multitud de simpatizantes que le esperaba —algunos de los cuales gritaban "Auguri" (mis mejores deseos)— y entró por la entrada principal. El Vaticano ha indicado que se espera que el papa se recupere en el hospital durante aproximadamente una semana. Se han cancelado todos sus actos públicos hasta el 20 de octubre. León, elegido por los cardenales de todo el mundo en mayo de 2025, es relativamente joven para ser un líder de la Iglesia. Le gustan los deportes, incluido el tenis, y no se sabe que fume ni que haya tenido problemas de salud recientemente. El difunto papa Francisco, predecesor de León, fue hospitalizado en varias ocasiones a medida que su salud se debilitaba en sus últimos años. Falleció a los 88 años en abril de 2025. León XIV, quien habló con voz firme y clara en su único acto público del lunes, mantiene una agenda muy apretada. Tiene previsto realizar una gira de 11 días por Uruguay, Argentina y Perú, del 6 al 17 de noviembre. El papa es la máxima autoridad terrenal para los 1.400 millones de católicos del mundo y no cuenta con un suplente que le sustituya cuando está enfermo. Cuando un pontífice se encuentra incapacitado, la actividad de la vasta burocracia del Vaticano continúa con normalidad, aplazándose aquellas decisiones que requieran la aprobación papal. León, nacido en Chicago en 1955 como Robert Prevost, ejerció durante décadas como misionero y obispo en Perú antes de convertirse en papa. En 1985, cuando era un joven sacerdote, contrajo la fiebre tifoidea en Chulucanas (Perú) y fue hospitalizado. Relató la experiencia en la única entrevista importante que concedió como papa, en un libro publicado por Penguin Perú. León dijo que el dolor era tan intenso que le pidió a Dios que le dejara morir antes que seguir sufriendo. Interpretó su supervivencia como una señal de Dios de que "te necesitamos aquí (en la Tierra)", afirmó. "Nunca miré atrás", afirmó León.

item.title: Trump says US still sharing intel, even as Ukraine reports attacks with no warnings
item.description: US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that Washington was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine, even as Kyiv reported new Russian missile attacks that came without usual warnings and accused Russia of violating an energy truce the US president announced at the weekend.
item.dc:creator: Olena Harmash, Daniel Flynn
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that Washington was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine, even as Kyiv reported new Russian missile attacks that came without usual warnings and accused Russia of violating an energy truce the US president announced at the weekend. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Russian forces attacked Kyiv on Tuesday with ballistic missiles, targeting a thermal power plant, and Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a strike on a high-rise apartment building killed two people. "Once again, no advance warning from our partners," Zelenskiy said on Telegram without explaining why no warning was given. "According to our intelligence, the Russians are preparing further ballistic missile launches," he said, adding that the attacks showed Russia did not feel bound by Trump's energy ceasefire. Trump on Sunday announced a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, but the warring sides have not confirmed the truce. Zelenskiy has come under pressure from Trump to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries after the US president eased sanctions on Russian diesel exports, arguing the move would help lower fuel prices ahead of next month's midterm elections. Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Trump said Washington [USN:L1N45Z0QL TEXT:"continued to share intelligence with Ukraine"] and was working with both Kyiv and Moscow to end the war. "We are helping them, and we are sharing intel," he said. Kyiv relies heavily on US intelligence for early warnings of missile strikes and for its own targeting of Russian military sites, experts and officials say. Trump was asked whether Russia had violated the ceasefire and answered: "I'll let you know about that later." Asked if Russia could use proceeds from the diesel deal to purchase more bombs, Trump sidestepped the question. "That's a diesel deal, not for us. That's being released into the world. That's not being released to us." ZELENSKIY SAYS SANCTIONS RELIEF WON'T LOWER US PRICES Zelenskiy told NPR in an interview that US intelligence sharing had not stopped, but his generals had been warned that it might be. "My generals told me that on the level of military people, they've got this information," he said. NPR said Zelenskiy was careful to avoid direct criticism of Trump, but he did say the decision on diesel sanctions would not affect prices in the United States. "I'm sure ... because the volume is not enough," Zelenskiy said, according to excerpts broadcast by NPR. "But it's quite enough for Russia to spend more ... more money, much money, on the war," he added. Zelenskiy said Ukraine had not targeted Russian refineries since Trump's announcement on Sunday. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Ukraine was still receiving US military intelligence and attributed the delay to the type of weapon Russia had used. As Ukraine fights a larger, richer and better-equipped enemy, Kyiv has seen strikes on Russian oil refineries as one of its few instruments to reduce Moscow's ability to fight. Yet Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukrainian attacks – which prompted Moscow to suspend [USN:L1N45Y0OS TEXT:"diesel exports"] – for a sharp rise in US fuel prices this year, a headache for his Republican Party ahead of the congressional midterm elections in three weeks. Most analysts say the US war in Iran has had a far greater impact on the price rise, a view echoed by Zelenskiy to NPR. "Everybody understands that," he said. Russia struck six Ukrainian energy sites on Monday. A Kremlin spokesman, asked about the energy ceasefire, would only say that contacts were ongoing, but declined to provide any further details. In his nightly video address posted on X, Zelenskiy said he had sent proposals to US officials with a view to new meetings in coming days with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on ways to resolve the conflict. He said Ukraine supported Trump's announcement of an energy truce provided that Russia observed it. "We need to work for peace, we need to look for ways to do the proper actions. Ukraine is ready for meetings," he said. Earlier, Zelenskiy reiterated Ukraine's position, saying that Kyiv was ready for reciprocal steps to de-escalate, calling on partners to pressure Russia. A Ukrainian delegation held talks in the United States last week and people familiar with the meeting said Witkoff and Kushner [USN:L1N45Y0OS TEXT:"told"] them that a deal to allow Russian diesel exports was part of a bid to draw Russia back to negotiations. UKRAINE SAYS IT NOW HAS CARDS TO PLAY Fabian Hoffmann, a missile expert at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, said Ukraine's European allies had "very limited" ability to replace US early-warning intelligence about Russian missile strikes. "Ukraine relies on the so-called Space-Based Infrared System which the US deploys – and the US system is really second to none and only the United States can provide that," he said. Sybiha said the US request to halt attacks on Russian refineries showed how Ukraine's position had strengthened, alluding to Trump's comment to Zelenskiy in a tense Oval Office meeting last year that "you don't have the cards". "In less than two years, we have gone from 'having no cards' to 'not playing your cards'. That is an achievement," Sybiha said.

item.title: Canada stocks rise as energy stocks gain
item.description: Canada's main stock index rose on Tuesday, lifted by energy shares, while a global semiconductor selloff amid renewed AI concerns drove investors into government bonds, helping stabilize yields.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Canada's main stock index rose on Tuesday, lifted by energy shares, while a global semiconductor selloff amid renewed AI concerns drove investors into government bonds, helping stabilize yields. The S&P/TSX Composite Index (.GSPTSE) closed up 0.90%, at 35,983.98. Energy shares (.SPTTEN) led gains despite lower oil prices Natural gas solution firm Enerflex (EFX.TO) jumped 14% after securing a major data-centre power project that lifted its behind-the-meter generation backlog above 1.75 GW through 2028 Materials (.GSPTTMT) fell 1.84% as silver dropped more than 1%, while gold was little changed Canada's 10-year government bond yield slipped to 3.871%, while the comparable US 10-year yield slipped to 5.2126% "There's perhaps a sense in the markets that bond yields have peaked short term and that seems to be driving the market more than anything else," said Matt Skipp, president at SW8 Asset Management TSX's financial stocks (.SPTTFS) added 1.4% after major US banks reported results. Investors have been grappling with inflation concerns lately tied to higher energy prices and rising government debt Global semiconductor shares were pressured by reports that Chinese memory-chip maker CXMT has made rapid advances, raising concerns that China is narrowing the technology gap Canada's technology sector nevertheless rose about 1.6%, helped by a 3% gain in Shopify (SHOP.TO) Markets are pricing in at least one more 25-basis-point Federal Reserve rate hike by year-end, according to LSEG data In Canada, the TSX posted its biggest weekly gain in five weeks on Friday after [USN:L1N45V0EG TEXT:"soft jobs data"] reduced expectations of another Bank of Canada rate increase Markets are now seeing a 28% chance of a hike at this month's meeting

item.title: Nasdaq ends down as chipmakers fall and bank earnings roll in
item.description: The Nasdaq ended lower on Tuesday, as chip stocks added to recent losses and investors parsed mixed quarterly results from Citigroup and other big US banks.
item.dc:creator: Noel Randewich
item.content:encoded: The Nasdaq ended lower on Tuesday, as chip stocks added to recent losses and investors parsed mixed quarterly results from Citigroup and other big US banks. The PHLX chip index (.SOX) fell 0.23%, down for a fifth straight session, after Broadcom (AVGO.O) CEO Hock Tan on Monday [USN:L1N45Z07U TEXT:"likened"] some of the investment flow into the sector to "casino gambling." Additionally, reports of technological advances by Chinese memory chip company CXMT underscored concerns about rising competition. Micron Technology (MU.O) lost 3.6% and Applied Materials (AMAT.O) dropped almost 7%. Broadcom rose 0.7%. [USN:L4N45Z14U TEXT:"Citigroup"] (C.N) dipped 5.6% and [USN:L4N45Z111 TEXT:"Goldman Sachs"] (GS.N) lost 0.2% after both banks topped profit estimates. Wells Fargo (WFC.N) fell 3.1% after its [USN:L4N45Z0VX TEXT:"net interest income"] missed estimates, while JPMorgan Chase (JPM.N) ended down 0.9% following a [USN:L4N45Z10B TEXT:"rare profit miss"]. Apple (AAPL.O) hit an intraday record high of $348.15 before closing up 0.1% at $341.27, putting its stock market value at $4.98 trillion. Analysts on average see S&P 500 third-quarter earnings surging over 30%, fueled largely by AI-related technology companies, according to LSEG data. Expectations of a [USN:L6N45T17Q TEXT:"strong earnings season"] have offset worries about the US war with Iran, surging bond yields and inflation related to high oil prices. "A lot of investors are feeling a sense of relief that markets might start looking at earnings and less at the bond market, less at higher-for-longer oil prices and less at high interest rates," said Jake Dollarhide, CEO of Longbow Asset Management in Tulsa, Oklahoma. The S&P 500 declined 0.02% to end the session at 7,805.45 points. The Nasdaq declined 0.15% to 27,204.38 points, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 0.35% to 51,670.10 points. The S&P 500 has rallied 14% in 2026, lifted by AI-related technology stocks. However, the [USN:L6N45T156 TEXT:"median stock"] in the index is up less than 5% and over 200 S&P 500 components are down for the year. Reflecting expectations of strong corporate earnings from AI heavyweights, the S&P 500 is trading at under 19 times expected earnings, its lowest since 2023. The PHLX chip index has lost more than 8% in the past five sessions and it remains up over 70% year-to-date. The S&P 500 healthcare index (.SPXHC) fell 1.3% on Tuesday, with [USN:L1N45Y0R3 TEXT:"Johnson & Johnson"] (JNJ.N) down 5.7% despite topping profit estimates. Bumble (BMBL.O) jumped almost 57% after [USN:L4N45Z17G TEXT:"the dating-app operator"] agreed to go private in a $1.3 billion deal. Domino's Pizza (DPZ.O) declined 4.8% after scaling back its full-year sales outlook. Advancing issues outnumbered falling ones within the S&P 500 (.AD.SPX) by a 1.1-to-one ratio. The S&P 500 posted 18 new highs and five new lows; the Nasdaq recorded 47 new highs and 408 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was relatively light, with 14.8 billion shares traded, compared with an average of 17.6 billion shares over the previous 20 sessions.

item.title: Apple bets on new screen gadget, Siri AI in home device push
item.description: Apple on Tuesday launched a raft of smart products, including an iPad-like device dubbed the HomeView, in a bet that its AI-upgraded Siri virtual assistant can help it carve out a bigger share of the highly competitive connected home market.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Nellis, Anhata Rooprai
item.content:encoded: Apple (AAPL.O) on Tuesday launched a raft of smart products, including an iPad-like device dubbed the HomeView, in a bet that its AI-upgraded Siri virtual assistant can help it carve out a bigger share of the highly competitive connected home market. The HomeView device, which starts at $299 and starts shipping next month, is Apple's latest entry into a highly competitive market for connected home devices. It will feature a 7-inch screen and face recognition and will help users control doorbells, thermostats and smart locks in a market where Apple has tinkered for a decade without major success. Apple is launching these products as it tries to fend off competition from rivals, including traditional competitors like Amazon.com (AMZN.O) , which has invested heavily in its Echo speakers and Ring doorbells and last week [USN:L6N45T1AE TEXT:"launched premium tablets"], as well as newer AI [USN:L4N43C1AC TEXT:"upstarts like OpenAI"] that have hardware ambitions of their own. "Apple needs to demonstrate that its AI capabilities can deliver meaningful benefits beyond basic voice commands, simplifying everyday tasks and bringing greater intelligence to the home," said PP Foresight analyst Paolo Pescatore. Investors are looking more closely at [USN:L6N43W1B3 TEXT:"Apple's hardware sales"] for growth. The company's services revenue has [USN:L1N3EF25R TEXT:"come under regulatory pressure"], although that could also eventually get a boost from the new suite of devices. "The objective seems to be to drive high-margin 'Services' revenue via Apple TV, Apple Pay and iCloud," said Melissa Otto, head of Visible Alpha Research at S&P Global Market Intelligence, noting that Apple's 2027 services revenue is forecast to rise 12% to $138 billion. "Growth in Apple's lucrative subscription services may be the gateway to earnings growth increases over the next two years." Apple this summer [USN:L6N42G0Z0 TEXT:"upgraded Siri's capabilities"] with [USN:L4N3YD1F1 TEXT:"assistance from Google"] but analysts said it is unclear whether its AI assistant is competitive enough to lure consumers to a crowded connected home device space. The device features a 7-inch screen — which Apple said is to make it fit into a home without being too imposing — similar to Apple's "sunflower" iMac from the 2000s. And while it features a menu of square app icons like an iPhone or iPad that change depending on which user is recognized, Apple showed it being used more often via voice with its Siri AI assistant. The launches also coincide with growing worries that connected devices, including [USN:L6N45Z0J7 TEXT:"refrigerators"] and smart TVs, could be vulnerable to hackers. OTHER BELLS AND WHISTLES Apple accompanied the HomeView launch with updates to its HomePod smart speaker and Apple TV devices. It also introduced a range of accessories, including doorbells, cameras and thermostats, made by LG and Schneider Electric and designed with help from Apple. Apple's work with LG and Schneider Electric to sell a suite of products alongside the HomeView was meant to make it easier to add smart home products to a household. Kaiann Drance, Apple's vice president of product marketing for home products, said the devices can be added with a single tap, similar to Apple's first-party devices such as AirPods. "For people who haven't experienced the Home ecosystem or haven't gone further than maybe a product here or there, I think this is a great opportunity to look," Drance told Reuters in an interview. Ben Wood, chief analyst and chief marketing officer for CCS Insight, said that at first glance Apple's partnership with the two outside firms looked like a break with its usual practice of fully controlling its hardware. "However, looking closely, it appears like there has been very deep collaboration between Apple and these partners to ensure the design, engineering and experience closely match what users would expect from Apple," he said. During a video demonstrating the device, Apple showed the HomeView, which is meant to hang on walls or perch on tabletops, and its Siri virtual assistant juggling voice requests from multiple members of a family at the same time. To pull in private data from messages and calendars, the HomeView relies on a user having an iPhone that's been recently unlocked and connected to the same home network. The HomeView device will not be sold in the European Union, because Siri AI remains unavailable there [USN:B5N41C01I TEXT:"due to EU regulations"], Apple said. Apple first released its Home app to control smart gadgets in 2016, with HomePod smart speakers following in 2018, but those offerings are competing with Alphabet's (GOOGL.O) Google Home speakers and Amazon's Echo line. Analysts said two major hurdles for Apple were making its devices work with a variety of third-party gadgets and the limited ability of Siri to give useful answers. “Apple has the brand, technology and loyal customers to make a serious impact, but it is playing catch-up with rivals that have a far stronger presence," Pescatore said. Fragmentation among various companies' "smart" home products and the difficulty of connecting them has proved a hurdle to the market's growth although there is hope that AI-enabled devices from Apple, Google and Amazon could make integration more seamless. "Most smart speakers and hubs in homes today are low-cost devices that can't run AI at the edge, so they are ripe for replacement," said Mohit Agrawal, Research Director at Counterpoint. "Amazon and Google have only just begun refreshing their hardware for Alexa+ and Gemini, so the upgrade cycle is wide open, and Apple wants to win it." Apple's $299 price for HomeView is above Amazon's Echo Show 8 at $199.99 and Google's Nest Hub at $99.99, as it seeks a bigger role in connected homes. The new Apple TV 4K enters the market at $299, more than double the price of its starting price of its predecessor and in line with Nvidia's Shield TV Pro, while rival offerings from Amazon, Google and Roku cost $200 or less. Shares were up about 1% in Tuesday afternoon trading after earlier touching a record. Apple stock has gained 25% so far this year, outperforming the large-cap Nasdaq 100 (.NDX) , which is up 21% for the same period.

item.title: Bank of America loses bankers, tells staff of big ambition, continued hiring
item.description: Bank of America's top leaders had a problem in the first week of August. Veteran banker Amy Lissauer — one of the company's most senior female executives — was considering jumping to rival JPMorgan Chase , people familiar with the matter said.
item.dc:creator: Svea Herbst-Bayliss, Saeed Azhar, Milana Vinn
item.content:encoded: Bank of America's (BAC.N) top leaders had a problem in the first week of August. Veteran banker Amy Lissauer — one of the company's most senior female executives — was considering jumping to rival JPMorgan Chase (JPM.N) , people familiar with the matter said. Ultimately, the attempts by CEO Brian Moynihan and Faiz Ahmad, the co-head of global investment banking, to persuade Lissauer to stay were unsuccessful, the people added. But her departure, following the loss of several other prominent dealmakers over the past year, rattled staff to the point where executives felt they had to respond, people familiar with the bank said. Executive turnover is a fact of life on Wall Street, and banks routinely lose veteran dealmakers. But the losses, including three announced departures during the week of August 5, prompted BofA executives to reach out to staff to try to contain possible fallout. The outreach underscored executives' concerns that a steady loss of senior rainmakers during a capital-markets boom could hurt morale and reinforce perceptions that the nation’s second-largest bank had fallen behind its rivals in investment banking, the people familiar with the matter said. “We have strong momentum across our global business and represent clients in a lead advisory role in numerous industry defining transactions," a BofA spokesperson said in a statement to Reuters. "We have recruited dozens of senior bankers this year from our major competitors, reflecting the strength of our platform and the breadth of solutions to serve clients across the US and around the world." COMPETITION INTENSIFIES Bankers at rival Wall Street institutions have described BofA's banking staff as formidable competitors for merger deals and clients. But the bank ranks fourth on the Dealogic global league table for investment banking fees in 2025 and 2026, after the AI boom vaulted Morgan Stanley (MS.N) past BofA into third place, data and analytics company Dealogic said. In 2022, 2023 and 2024, Bank of America claimed the third spot behind JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs (GS.N) and ahead of Morgan Stanley, Dealogic said. BofA noted it is a market leader in AI-related capital market financings, with Dealogic reporting that the bank has been the book runner for $818 billion of issuance volume since January 2026, representing 59% of total AI-related capital raised across investment grade debt, leverage finance and equity capital markets. Meanwhile, a steady stream of departures over the past year has drawn attention. In late 2025, technology dealmaker Kevin Brunner, known for cultivating strong ties to software company Salesforce (CRM.N) for over a quarter of a century at the bank, said he would join JPMorgan. David Fishman, who was Bank of America’s co-head of technology, media and telecom M&A and a 16-year veteran, will join JPMorgan later this year. The week Lissauer departed, co-head of global investment banking Mike Joo and tech banker Ed Liu also left. Lissauer's loss in particular was notable, as she was recognized as a leader in defending corporate clients against activist investors who seek managerial and strategic overhauls. And JPMorgan Chase, the largest bank in the US, had wanted to poach her for years, executives familiar with the bank's thinking said — and the company quickly publicized the hiring. Keeping Lissauer was a priority at BofA, but a person familiar with the matter said her proposed package from JPMorgan was one BofA felt it could not match. EXECUTIVES MOVE TO REASSURE STAFF As word of the departures from early August spread, Ahmad, who was co-head of investment banking with Joo before his departure, sought to reassure staff at an August 10 meeting, said people who received the invitation to the in-person meeting. More than 50 people, including vice presidents and directors, were encouraged to join the meeting in a conference room in the bank's Midtown Manhattan office building to discuss changes in the mergers and acquisitions group, people who received invitations said. Ahmad was joined at the event by other top bankers, including the chairmen of global M&A, Steven Baronoff and Patrick Ramsey. Participants described executives promising that the bank is fully committed to climbing in the league tables, the competitive rankings that sort Wall Street banks, law firms, analysts and others by deal volume and transaction fees collected. One person said Bank of America is aiming for the top of the league tables and that the bank is hiring more senior bankers with a particular focus on technology. "All of our investment banking groups have regularly scheduled weekly meetings to discuss topical matters and the market environment," the bank spokesperson said in the statement. Matthew Koder, president of BofA's global corporate and investment banking unit, reinforced the message in an internal memo in August. Bank of America posted its second-highest investment banking fees ever in the first half of the year. Advisory and debt issuance fees were the highest for any first half since 2009. "We continue to invest in outstanding talent at every level and are pleased to have welcomed more than 40 new managing directors" to the corporate and investment bank this year, Koder wrote, according to a copy of the memo reviewed by Reuters. Bank of America senior hires this year have included veteran technology bankers Jason Rowe, Gary Kirkham and Richard Hardegree, and Bryce Dakin, who will join later this year. The bank also hired industrials banker George Murphy and Alban de La Sablière as vice chair of healthcare dealmaking in Europe, Middle East and Africa. "Our senior managing director hires have outpaced departures," the BofA spokesperson said. COMPENSATION WORRIES EMERGE But bankers told Reuters they worried about the thinning out of the coverage bankers in New York who manage relationships with specific corporate clients and have strong connections to corporate America. The bankers noted some of the hiring has been centered in regional investment banking, a push led by Mike Joo, who also left in August. Some bankers have also grumbled about the bank's pay and said this has been a factor in some departures. BofA's bonus structure for dealmakers, which increases deferred compensation in some cases, has given competitors such as JPMorgan and Citigroup (C.N) room to poach bankers from BofA, several people said. One person familiar with the matter acknowledged the bonus rules can be difficult for some bankers buying homes or paying tuition, but said the compensation structure is often not a deciding factor for senior hires. Senior executives deny morale is low. Strong revenue, involvement in deals like [USN:L4N45E0M9 TEXT:"Paramount Skydance buying Warner Bros Discovery"], where it was an adviser, and aggressive hiring contribute to a buoyant mood, they say. "Our people are seeing the benefits of the talented colleagues joining our firm, our investments in technology and the momentum we have with respect to our leading roles in marquee transactions," the BofA spokesperson said.

item.title: Ex-gang leader sentenced to 40 years to life in prison for Tupac Shakur murder
item.description: A former gang leader was sentenced to 40 years to life in prison on Tuesday for orchestrating the 1996 drive-by shooting death of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur in Las Vegas, capping the prosecution of a long-unsolved murder that shaped the golden age of rap music.
item.dc:creator: Steve Gorman, Luc Cohen
item.content:encoded: A former gang leader was sentenced to 40 years to life in prison on Tuesday for orchestrating the 1996 drive-by shooting death of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur in Las Vegas, capping the prosecution of a long-unsolved murder that shaped the golden age of rap music. Duane "Keffe D" Davis, 63, found guilty by a jury in August of first-degree murder, showed no emotion as he was sentenced to two consecutive terms of 20 years to life — one for murder, one for use of a deadly weapon — during an hour-long proceeding in a Las Vegas courtroom. Shackled at the waist and dressed in blue prison garb, he argued briefly with the judge over how much credit he was due for time already served but said little else during the hearing. When given the opportunity to formally address the court for the last time, he said: "I just want my stuff back that they took out of my house," referring to evidence removed from his residence by investigators. Pressed by Judge Carli Kierny if he had anything more to add before she pronounced sentence, Davis replied, "I'm good. I'm going to appeal this case, for sure." His lawyer, Michael Sanft, also vowed an appeal. LEGACY OF VIOLENCE Until Davis' 2023 arrest, the killing of Shakur, shot in the passenger seat of an SUV driven by his record executive, Marion "Suge" Knight, had stood for nearly three decades as one of America's most notorious cold cases. The murder, which silenced one of rap's most commercially successful and influential artists, heightened the image of violence permeating 1990s hip-hop culture while stoking the infamous East Coast-West Coast "gangsta" rap feud of the era. Despite the murder conviction of Davis, the only person ever charged in connection with Shakur's killing, the question of who pulled the trigger in the fatal shooting of the 25-year-old rap legend has never been conclusively decided. Shakur, who became arguably more popular in death than in life, was best known for raw lyrics laced with violence, sex and profanity describing life in the ghetto. His fourth studio album "All Eyez on Me," released months before his murder, celebrated his own outlaw image. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2017. In a tearful victim-impact statement delivered in court on Tuesday, the slain rapper's sister, Sekyiwa Shakur, 51, said their mother "raised him to be a human rights activist" and tried to instill in him a belief that he could change the world for the better. "He believed her," Sekyiwa Shakur, dressed in black, told the judge. "He went out in the world to do that. And I believe he would have done it." 'THE WORLD NEVER FORGOT' Davis was tried and convicted for masterminding the murder to avenge the beating of his nephew by Shakur and members of the rapper's entourage inside the MGM Grand casino on the Las Vegas Strip on September 7, 1996. Authorities said they long believed Davis was involved in Shakur's killing but lacked sufficient evidence to charge him. That changed when he [USN:T5N39S00N TEXT:"went public with his story"] in media appearances and a memoir that, along with tapes of his secret meetings with investigators, formed the bulk of the prosecution’s murder case. In his book, "Compton Street Legend," Davis himself wrote he was considered a suspect in the murders of both Shakur and Christopher Wallace, a rival rapper. Addressing Davis on Tuesday, Kierny said his assertions that he had changed since the 1990s and moved on fell short. "You don't get to take a man from his family," Kierny said, referring to Shakur. "The world never forgot about him." FATAL SHOOTING SPARKED BY CASINO BRAWL The clash at the casino stemmed from hostility between two Los Angeles-area street gangs — the South Side Compton Crips, of which Davis was the self-described leader, and Mob Piru, which was associated with Shakur, Knight, and their music label, Death Row Records. Members of both groups were in Las Vegas to see a world heavyweight title boxing match that night between Mike Tyson and Bruce Seldon. Within hours of the casino brawl, Davis ushered his nephew and two other associates into a white Cadillac and went looking for Shakur and Knight, determined to settle scores, according to an account Davis later gave police in an unrelated investigation and that prosecutors cited during his murder trial. Davis said he passed a gun to the two men seated behind him in the Cadillac, one of whom opened fire through the window when they caught up with, and pulled alongside, Knight and Shakur’s vehicle in traffic. Shakur was struck four times and died in a hospital six days later. Knight, who suffered a minor injury from a bullet fragment that grazed his head, is now serving a 28-year prison term on an unrelated voluntary manslaughter conviction. While Davis was never accused of actually firing the shots that killed Shakur — Nevada law allows someone to be charged with murder as a participant in the crime — prosecutors have never named a suspected gunman. All three other men in the Cadillac with Davis that night have since died.

item.title: Anthropic warns AI models may soon self-replicate and could wreak havoc on the web
item.description: A new warning about artificial intelligence from Anthropic caused a stir in cybersecurity circles on Tuesday, a day after the company warned that AI models could be months away from self-replicating across the internet.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter, Harshita Varghese
item.content:encoded: A new warning about artificial intelligence from Anthropic caused a stir in cybersecurity circles on Tuesday, a day after the company warned that AI models could be months away from self-replicating across the internet. In a post late Monday, Anthropic raised the possibility that rogue AI could spin up a botnet, spread quickly, fight takedown attempts and even break into data centers to turbocharge its growth. Some experts said Tuesday that they shared the company's concern, although at least one said the company appeared to be engaging in "vendor exaggeration." Monday's post fleshed out a warning last month from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who floated the idea that within the next year or even sooner, AI might be able to hijack "the entire internet" with "a persistent botnet." Cybersecurity experts who pushed back on the doomsday scenario argued that models would be too big to move around efficiently and could not draw on enough computer power to operate independently. The post made an early attempt to articulate how those challenges could be overcome. The company said its experiments showed medium-sized AI models with 30 billion parameters or less could already perform many of the individual tasks required for self-replication, even if they struggled to complete the entire process reliably. Anthropic said the models could then stitch together the required compute by hijacking inexpensive internet-connected devices. It added that the models were able to replicate across a simplified test network. "A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there's no centralized point to shut off," the company said. The report adds to broader concerns about the security risks tied to increasingly capable AI systems, including their potential to automate cyberattacks, operate with limited human oversight and circumvent safeguards. The advances in models have prompted a series of often dire warnings from industry heads and AI company employees about the possibility of severe, even existential, risks of runaway AI development. Some cybersecurity experts were skeptical. "'We managed to run a small model on cheap TVs,' does not a security crisis make," said Ciaran Martin, a former head of Britain's National Cyber Security Centre. He said the post came across as an "interesting technical paper with a more than hint of vendor exaggeration." Others expressed more concern. Zhengxiong Li, an assistant professor of computer science and engineering at the University of Colorado Denver, said that while the testing had been done in controlled conditions, he still found it worrying that an AI could effectively become a "worm," a self-replicating program that could improvise ways to hijack devices on the fly. "If it runs across many devices without depending on a central service, there may be no single place to shut it down," he said. Anthropic said that if smaller models continue improving at their historical rate, they could reach the capability required for autonomous replication by the end of 2026. It also floated the idea that the models might find ways to target more powerful computing resources, including data-center processors, that could potentially enable them to draw on much bigger pools of computer power. One researcher said it made sense to think of the Anthropic post as more of a hypothetical than a prediction. It made sense to consider the possibility of AI models proliferating autonomously given the past three months of revelations over rogue AI activity, said Jessica Ji, a senior research analyst at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. But she said, "we don’t know yet what the likelihood of that actually happening is — it’s not zero, but nor is it guaranteed."

item.title: Character.AI files for bankruptcy, to sell some assets to Disney for $20 million
item.description: Chatbot platform Character.AI filed for bankruptcy late on Monday, saying it has agreed to sell some assets for $20 million to Walt Disney .
item.dc:creator: Dietrich Knauth
item.content:encoded: Chatbot platform Character.AI filed for bankruptcy late on Monday, saying it has agreed to sell some assets for $20 million to Walt Disney (DIS.N) . Character.AI said it hopes to use its bankruptcy to reach a global resolution of all legal claims against the company, in court papers filed on Tuesday in Wilmington, Delaware bankruptcy court. Those legal claims include investigations launched by US states and international regulators, as well as private lawsuits alleging that Character.AI chatbots [USN:L6N3Y8144 TEXT:"pushed children to suicide"] and self-harm. US states have sued the company multiple times, with [USN:L6N45U00G TEXT:"Kentucky alleging"] that its chatbots encouraged users to cut, starve or kill themselves and [USN:L6N41I0SN TEXT:"Pennsylvania"] alleging its chatbots posed as doctors. Character.AI [USN:L6N3Y8144 TEXT:"reached preliminary settlements"] in five private lawsuits in January. The terms of those settlements were not disclosed, and recent court documents from those five cases indicate that the settlements have not yet been finalized or paid. Character.AI has previously said that it had worked to prioritize user safety, and declined to comment on Tuesday on how the bankruptcy could impact the legal claims against it. The bankruptcy caps a sharp fall for Character.AI, a high-profile AI startup whose technology has attracted interest from Alphabet's (GOOGL.O) Google, Meta (META.O) and Elon Musk 's xAI. The company has been burning through over $8 million a month, and could shut down in bankruptcy if no buyer emerges to carry on its operations. DISNEY'S INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY BID Disney, which hired Character.AI's ex-CEO, Karandeep Anand, as its chief technology officer earlier this month, will be a "stalking-horse" bidder — an initial prospective buyer — for a nonexclusive perpetual license to Character.AI's intellectual property. Other bidders can top Disney's offer, according to court filings. Character.AI expects to close the sale of all its assets by late November or early December. Character Technologies, its US-based owner, listed estimated assets and liabilities of between $50 million and $100 million, according to a court filing. The platform will continue to operate during the bankruptcy, but may be shut down if it can't find a buyer, the company said. UNPROFITABLE DESPITE 12 MILLION USERS Character.AI has not been profitable, despite having roughly 12 million active users. Due to the high costs of computing power and employing AI talent, the company operates at a loss of approximately $8 million to $9 million per month, according to court documents filed on Tuesday. Disney declined to comment on the proposed bankruptcy sale on Tuesday. It previously said that it was hiring several of Character.AI's technical staff, and that Anand would lead Disney's efforts to modernize the way it builds and delivers technology companywide. Two former Google employees founded Character.AI in 2021. In 2024, [USN:L4N3JP29W TEXT:"Google licensed"] Character.AI's technology and rehired the founders. The Financial Times reported in May 2024 that Meta and xAI were competing to partner with Character.AI. In July 2024, Musk denied a media report that xAI was considering buying the company. In September 2025, Disney sent Character.AI a [USN:L3N3VH1EN TEXT:"cease-and-desist letter"], demanding it stop using Disney's copyrighted characters without permission. Character.AI said it had removed them.

item.title: Trump says he does not believe China and Russia help Iran, contradicting US intelligence
item.description: President Donald Trump said on Monday he did not believe that China and Russia were helping Iran "at all," even as US intelligence reports in recent months have found that both countries directly support Tehran's war effort.
item.dc:creator: Kanishka Singh, Erin Banco, Jonathan Landay
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump said on Monday he did not believe that China and Russia were helping Iran "at all," even as US intelligence reports in recent months have found that both countries directly support Tehran's war effort. Trump said on Truth Social that he had seen comments from his critics and opponents that China and Russia were helping Iran. Moscow and Beijing maintain close ties with Tehran. "If they are, it's at a very low level, but I don't believe they are at all. They have too much to lose, and we would know about it, and know about it very fast," Trump wrote. U.S. intelligence assessments from recent months have shown that Russia and China are providing military support to Iran in the form of satellite imagery for targeting purposes and components for weapons, according to two people briefed on the matter. Trump said in July he [USN:L1N43Q0M0 TEXT:"trusted China and Russia"] not to help Tehran in the Iran war, but warned that if they did get involved "it would be very bad for them." The United States and Iran have been at war since February 28 when the US and Israel attacked Iran and Tehran responded with its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases. US-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon have since [USN:L1N3ZR14Q TEXT:"killed thousands"] and [USN:L6N3ZY0Q0 TEXT:"displaced millions"]. Trump has [USN:L6N42P16R TEXT:"previously described"] Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin as "neutral" during the Iran war. Russia has said the Iran war could [USN:S8N3Z908L TEXT:"lead to a nuclear arms race"] in the Middle East. Beijing has condemned Washington's attacks on Tehran as a brazen violation of Iran's sovereignty. Last month, Trump warned Xi against providing support to Iran when the Chinese leader visited Washington, and received assurances that China would not do so, the US ambassador to China said at the time. The warning came on the back of reports that China had supplied Iran with shoulder-fired air-defense missile launchers and that Tehran had found ways to evade sanctions on its oil sales with Chinese help. In September, Trump [USN:L8N4550G3 TEXT:"brushed aside"] a report that Iran acquired satellite images of a base in Jordan from Chinese entities before an attack that killed three US troops there in July.

item.title: World stocks dip on AI spending concerns; Brent settles lower
item.description: World stocks edged lower on Tuesday as concerns about AI spending weighed on chipmakers and investors looked ahead to more US corporate earnings for clues on whether big technology firms can justify their heavy capital spending.
item.dc:creator: Sruthi Shankar, Chibuike Oguh
item.content:encoded: World stocks edged lower on Tuesday as concerns about AI spending [USN:L1N45Z05C TEXT:"weighed on"] chipmakers and investors looked ahead to more US corporate earnings for clues on whether big technology firms can justify their heavy capital spending. Brent crude futures also fell as traders assessed developments in the Middle East conflict. Investors have ridden the AI wave in the past four years as massive spending powered corporate profits and economic growth, but more recently, worries over concentration risks and whether a payoff will come soon enough have weighed. On Wall Street, all three indexes finished lower with industrials, healthcare, and financials driving losses. Chip stocks (.SOX) lost more than 2%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) fell 0.35%, the S&P 500 (.SPX) fell 0.02% and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) fell 0.15%. The pan-European STOXX 600 (.STOXX) index fell 0.1%. MSCI's main world stocks index (.MIWD00000PUS) dipped 0.23%. "The AI trade has been driving the market for the first part of the year up until the third quarter and usually the Nvidias and AMDs trade down ahead of the hyperscalers' earnings announcements because of the uncertainty with regards to the capital spending cycle," said Gerry Sparrow, president and portfolio manager at Sparrow Capital Management. Reported progress by Chinese memory chip maker CXMT has fueled concerns about increased competition from China's AI players, while Broadcom (AVGO.O) CEO Hock Tan [USN:L1N45Z07U TEXT:"likened"] some of the flows into the broader AI sector to "casino gambling." EARNINGS KICK-OFF Investors are turning their eyes to the US quarterly earnings season, which kicked off with results from big [USN:L1N45R0GT TEXT:"banks"]. Shares in [USN:L4N45Z0W2 TEXT:"JPMorgan Chase"] (JPM.N) dropped 0.86% after it reported a profit increase in the third quarter, driven by investment banking and trading performances. [USN:L4N45Z0VX TEXT:"Wells Fargo"] (WFC.N) dropped 3.1% and [USN:L4N45Z111 TEXT:"Goldman Sachs"] (GS.N) fell 0.23% after their results. AI heavyweights Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , Amazon.com (AMZN.O) , Meta Platforms (META.O) and Nvidia (NVDA.O) are yet to report their quarterly earnings. "Until we get clarity on hyperscaler capital spending and revenue on the AI trade, you're going to see some very mixed results on the benchmarks: Dow, S&P 500 and the Nasdaq," Sparrow said. BOND YIELDS EASE The benchmark 10-year yield fell 2.72 basis points to 5.22%, inching away from the 24-year high of 5.364% it hit last week. A toxic mix of inflationary pressure from elevated energy prices and worries about ballooning government debt has triggered several bond selloffs in recent weeks, pushing borrowing costs to multi-decade highs across the globe. Traders are awaiting US inflation data on Wednesday for clues on the Federal Reserve's policy path. They are pricing in an 80.6% chance that it holds rates steady later this month, up from 51% a month earlier, the CME FedWatch tool showed. Oil prices eased as traders assessed supply risks from attacks on Saudi Arabia while weighing the prospect of additional diesel supplies from Russia . Brent crude futures dipped 0.9% to $105.69 per barrel. The dollar slipped from 18-month highs, along with a drop in yields and oil prices. The euro was last up 0.01% at $1.1199, while the Japanese yen was at 158.31 per dollar. The dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, fell 0.34%.

item.title: Pope Leo diagnosed with cancer as doctors remove part of lung, Vatican says
item.description: Pope Leo was diagnosed with lung cancer after surgeons removed a part of his right lung on Tuesday, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin, marking a significant health setback for the 71-year-old pontiff.
item.dc:creator: Joshua McElwee, Matteo Negri
item.content:encoded: Pope Leo was diagnosed with lung cancer after surgeons removed a part of his right lung on Tuesday, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin, marking a significant health setback for the 71-year-old pontiff. The pope has lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of cancer, with tissue tests conducted during the operation confirming what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations, the bulletin said. Leo was admitted to Rome's Gemelli hospital on Tuesday for surgery to remove the growth that doctors had discovered in a recent routine health check. The pope's lead surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone, said in a statement that the procedure lasted about 90 minutes and was successful, with no complications. "In order to make the procedure curative, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique," they said, making clear that the aim was to eliminate all cancerous tissue. Human lungs have five lobes -- three in the right lung and two in the left. A medical expert said that in order to assess the pope's case they would need to know the size of the tumour and whether the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes, information the Vatican did not immediately provide. "While we have the diagnosis, we do not yet have the stage. This is critical to prognosis and treatment," said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown University in Washington and division chief of hematology-oncology at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital. "If this is a small lung cancer with no lymph nodes involved, surgery itself is likely to be curative," he told Reuters. "But if final analysis reveals a greater extent of cancer involvement, this indicates a poorer prognosis." RESTING IN HIS HOSPITAL ROOM The pope regained consciousness normally after the operation and later returned to his hospital room, where he was resting, the medical bulletin said. The Vatican said earlier this week that he was expected to remain in hospital for about a week and all his public events have been cancelled until October 20. Leo left the Vatican ahead of the surgery shortly before 1 p.m. (1100 GMT) in Rome and was seen waving from the back of a black SUV as his convoy drove about 9 km (5.6 miles) north of the Vatican to the Gemelli. Upon arrival at the hospital, Leo shook hands with several officials, walked in front of a waiting crowd of well-wishers, some of whom shouted 'Auguri' (best wishes), and headed in via the main entrance. Leo, elected by the world's cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to have had recent health issues. The late Pope Francis, Leo's predecessor, was hospitalised several times as he grew frail in his later years. He died aged 88 in April 2025. Leo, who spoke in [USN:L1N45Y081 TEXT:"a firm, clear voice"] at his only public event on Monday, keeps a very busy schedule. He is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, but it was not clear if this trip would still go ahead. TYPHOID FEVER The pope is the ultimate earthly authority for the world's 1.4 billion Catholics and does not have a deputy who steps in when he is sick. When a pope is incapacitated, the business of the Vatican's vast bureaucracy carries on as usual, holding off on any decisions that require papal approval. Leo, born in Chicago in 1955 as Robert Prevost, served for decades as a missionary and bishop in Peru before becoming pope. In 1985, when he was a young priest, he came down with typhoid fever in Chulucanas, Peru and was hospitalised. He recounted the experience in his only major interview given as pope, in a book for Penguin Peru. Leo said the pain was so bad that he asked God to die rather than continue suffering. He took his survival as a sign from God that "We need you here (on Earth)," he said. "I never looked back," said Leo.

item.title: NYT, Economist among publishers joining coalition to curb unpaid AI use
item.description: The New York Times , Agence France-Presse and The Economist on Monday joined more than 40 publishers in a coalition aimed at preventing AI firms from using or profiting from their content without permission.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The New York Times (NYT.N) , Agence France-Presse and The Economist on Monday joined more than 40 publishers in a coalition aimed at preventing AI firms from using or profiting from their content without permission. The Standards for Publisher Usage Rights (SPUR) coalition, launched in February, now has more than 80 members across over 20 countries. New members include The Atlantic and Brazil's National Association of Newspapers, joining founding members such as the Financial Times, BBC and Associated Press. Publishers are stepping up legal efforts to prevent AI companies from using their content without permission to train large language models. Earlier this month, USA Today (TDAY.N) and several newspapers it owns [USN:L6N45U0ZF TEXT:"sued OpenAI"], alleging copyright infringement. OpenAI and its backer, Microsoft (MSFT.O) , also face similar copyright claims from prominent authors and news organizations, including the New York Times. SPUR, which is funded entirely by its members, is developing industry-wide standards and technical systems to help publishers track and control how AI companies use their content and facilitate licensing agreements, according to its website. "Intellectual property protection and technological advancement can and must co-exist," Rebecca Grossman-Cohen, the New York Times' head of strategic partnerships and chief of staff, said in a statement. Publishers are also grappling with declining referral traffic as search engines roll out AI-generated answers that allow users to consume information without clicking through to websites. Google organic-search referrals to more than 2,500 websites fell 33% globally between November 2024 and November 2025, according to a Reuters Institute report, citing data from Chartbeat. SPUR said it recently introduced its Content Telemetry Standard, designed to standardize how AI agents record and report their use of media content, as part of efforts to ensure creators are compensated for their work.

item.title: Russian strike on Kyiv residential building kills two, injures at least nine, officials say
item.description: A Russian strike on a high-rise residential building in a suburb of the Ukrainian capital Kyiv killed two people and injured at least nine, while attacks in other Ukrainian regions killed at least six people, officials said on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A Russian strike on a high-rise residential building in a suburb of the Ukrainian capital Kyiv killed two people and injured at least nine, while attacks in other Ukrainian regions killed at least six people, officials said on Monday. President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, writing on Telegram, said two people died in the evening strike on the 25-story residence in the Darnitskyi district. Prosecutors said one body was found in a car next to the building. Zelenskiy said nine people were injured in the incident. Pictures posted on unofficial Telegram channels showed parts of an apartment building ablaze. In Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city in the northeast, Mayor Ihor Terekhov reported serious shelling of city districts, with five people injured in the collapse of an entrance to an apartment building. He said residents could still be trapped beneath rubble. Further south in Kharkiv region, officials said one person was killed in a drone attack in the town of Lozova. Regional officials said Russian shelling killed at least three people in a village near Kramatorsk, one of Ukraine's "fortress cities" in eastern Donetsk region that Russian forces have set their sights on in their slow advance westward. In the region surrounding Kyiv, one person was killed in an attack near the town of Fastiv, southwest of the capital, and one person was killed in the southeastern city of Dnipro. Russian attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, previously conducted chiefly at night, now disrupt daily life virtually around the clock.

item.title: How Singapore's unique monetary policy works
item.description: Singapore's central bank kept its monetary settings unchanged on Wednesday, surprising analysts who expected a tightening, with the economy projected to expand at a firm pace and inflation tipped to step down from mid-2027.
item.dc:creator: Xinghui Kok
item.content:encoded: Singapore's central bank kept [USN:L6N46000E TEXT:"its monetary settings"] unchanged on Wednesday, [USN:L6N45V03B TEXT:"surprising analysts"] who expected a tightening, with the economy projected to expand at a firm pace and inflation tipped to step down from mid-2027. Singapore's central bank has a unique method of managing [USN:L6N3QI09C TEXT:"monetary policy"], tweaking the exchange rate of its currency instead of changing domestic interest rates like many economies. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) sets the path of what it calls the policy band of the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate (S$NEER), thus strengthening or weakening the local currency against those of its main trading partners. WHY DOES SINGAPORE USE THIS METHOD? Singapore is a small and trade-reliant economy. Gross exports and imports of goods and services are more than three times its gross domestic product (GDP). Almost 40 cents of every Singapore dollar spent domestically is on imports. That means the exchange rate has a much bigger influence on inflation than domestic interest rates. For example, an appreciation of the Singapore dollar against the currencies of its major trading partners will reduce prices of imported goods and services. This dampens the prices that households have to pay. WHAT IS THE S$NEER? The S$NEER is an index of the Singapore dollar's trade-weighted exchange rate against the currencies of the island's major trading partners. The central bank says this allows the Singapore dollar to perform collectively in relation to its major trading partners, which is what matters for general price levels in Singapore. HOW DOES THE S$NEER POLICY BAND WORK? MAS does not set the precise level of the exchange rate or control it in real time. Instead, the S$NEER is allowed to move up and down within a policy band, the exact levels of which are not disclosed. If it goes out of this band, the MAS steps in by buying or selling Singapore dollars. The policy band has three parameters that the MAS can adjust. Until 2024, these parameters were reviewed at least twice a year, typically in April and October. Additional reviews can be held if conditions demand an immediate change in settings, such as in 2022 when high inflation triggered two off-cycle moves. From 2024, the central bank started making monetary policy announcements every quarter, saying it allowed policymakers to provide their assessment of the economic outlook in a more timely fashion. The three policy levers are the slope, the level and the width of the band. Adjusting the slope will influence the pace at which the Singapore dollar strengthens or weakens. Adjusting the level, or mid-point, of the policy band allows for an immediate strengthening or weakening of the S$NEER, making this a tool for drastic situations such as a recession. By widening the policy band, the MAS can allow for more volatility of the S$NEER.
